newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Russia cuts gas supply to freezing Georgia, Armenia.
newsitem.headline: Russia cuts gas supply to freezing Georgia, Armenia.

text.p: Ex-Soviet Georgia and Armenia were cut off from vital natural gas supplies on Thursday over unpaid bills to a Russian-Turkmen state-owned joint venture.

Georgian state-run gas firm Gruztransgasprom said supplies from Russian-Turkmen state-owned venture ITERA, which supplies Georgia and neighbouring Armenia with Russian natural gas, stopped early Thursday morning.
The two republics usually receive supplies via single pipeline running through Russia from Central Asia.
Georgia relies on the gas supplies for 50 percent of power generating capacity during the winter, when hydrostations are idle in the mountainous country of five million.
The effect of the cut-off was immediately apparent as already scant electric supplies in Georgia became even more scarce.
Armenian Energy Ministry officials said they had ample reserves of gas and fuel oil for energy generating and that they saw no immediate effect from the cut-off.
Armenia has a nuclear power station which makes it less reliant on the imported gas. It recently concluded an agreement with Iran to hook up to its power grid.
Gruztransgasprom general director Ivan Zazashvili said the cut-off of the daily 4.5 million cubic metres to Georgia came with no warning.
"Usually in these situations, they give at least a week's notice. Instead of that, they called the day before (Tuesday) and said we wouldn't get more gas until we paid all the bills."
He said the gas was turned off on Wednesday. Supplies dried up in the capital Tbilisi early Thursday morning.
He said Georgia was paying arrears to the company according to an agreed timetable.
Nearly all Turkmen gas exports pass through the Russian gas pipeline network, giving Russia major influence over supplies.
ITERA, a gas marketing venture, worked with Russian natural gas monopoly Gazprom to set up the Turkmenrosgas venture in 1995 to export 60 billion cubic metres last year.

Most homes throughout Georgia are already on a strict winter regime and receive only four hours of power per day. Homes, even in Tbilisi, are often heated with wood stoves and meals cooked over kerosene heaters.
The situation on Thursday was even worse, with most homes not getting even the bare-bones scheduled two hours of electricity in the morning.

Armenian officials said the republic usually gets 5.5 million cubic metres of gas per day via the route but that this had been halted as well over their own unpaid bills. The amount of the arrears was not immediately known.

Georgian officials said it would be impossible for them to pay the back debts immediately because of unpaid bills by consumers and industry, but that they were considering the asking the Central Bank to make an interim loan so that supplies can be restored.
Deputy Energy Minister Revaz Arveladze told Reuters that Georgia owed ITERA $24 million for previous gas deliveries.
Arveladze said he thought worsening political relations between Georgia and Russia could have been partially responsible for the cut-off.
Russia last week said Georgian "terrorists" had detonated a remote-control mine, killing three of its servicemen in the rebel Georgian Black Sea region of Abkhazia.
Georgia lost a war to separatist forces there in 1993 and Russian peackeepers have patrolled part of it since.
